candidates.statement: TinyML performs inference under 1 mW; on-device/near-sensor inference avoids wireless transmission's higher energy cost.
Benchmarking TinyML is hard because of four coupled challenges: power-measurement scope, limited memory/quantization diversity, hardware heterogeneity, and software/toolchain heterogeneity.
CoreMark does not profile full programs or represent ML inference workloads.
MLMark uses real ML workloads but needs far more memory/runtime than MCUs provide and lacks power measurement.
MLPerf's inference suite excludes MCU-class platforms for lack of small benchmarks/implementations.
No existing benchmark characterizes accuracy-latency-energy tradeoffs for ultra-low-power inference; the authors state this gap directly.
The suite defines four reference benchmarks, each pairing a fixed dataset/model/threshold with a common latency-accuracy-energy harness.
The suite is modular so a submitter can show one stack layer's benefit against a shared baseline.
Closed/open divisions balance comparability and flexibility.
Latency, accuracy, and energy are each scored by a defined 5-run protocol, with anti-gaming rules for energy.
VWW: task rationale, ~86% reference accuracy, 80% closed-division threshold.
IC: task rationale, custom ResNetv1 design choices, 86.5% on 200 images, 85% threshold.
KWS: task rationale, 12-class design rationale, 92.2%/91.6%/91.7% accuracy figures, model-choice rationale, feature-extraction exclusion rationale, 90% threshold.
AD: task/dataset/model rationale, AUC-ROC metric rationale, 0.88/0.86 AUC figures, 0.85 threshold.
All four reference implementations ran on the reference board and met accuracy targets, with wide latency/energy spread (qualitative; underlying figure numbers unavailable).
The v0.5 round drew five results (4 closed, 1 open) across ARM MCU, RISC-V MCU, RasPi4, an accelerator, and an FPGA, each demonstrating a different stack layer.
Across submissions: INT8 dominant, frameworks ranged open-interpreter to hardware compiler, power spanned microwatts to watts.
No submission modified the training dataset, despite a general data-centric trend in AI.
The authors interpret the round as showing TinyML practice still concentrated on models/frameworks/hardware, not data.
The suite is already used as a standard TinyML task set and packaged into a public development-platform project.
Future/open items the authors themselves flag: streaming/pre-processing measurement, architectural coverage beyond FC/CNN, long-term stability, dual-use/e-waste risk.
